title: A Room for the Winter
premise: Folklorist Coral Ravensworth arrives in the snowbound village of Hollowmere to record its winter songs, which the villagers will sing only once and never repeat. He lodges in the old Ravensworth house he has inherited without knowing why it was left to him, and soon every mirror there reflects the room a second behind — showing things that have not happened yet. The songs are not folklore but the surviving verses of a ritual the village founders began generations ago: each winter they feed one outsider to the house so the rest may live. Coral learns he was not invited but chosen, and that his own family helped build the trap; yet the house offers him belonging if he completes the ritual willingly. In the end Coral sings the final verse himself — not to finish the founders' rite, but to reverse it, giving the house what it truly wanted all along: someone who remembers it honestly. The mirrors fall silent, the village is freed from its bargain, and Coral stays through the winter as the house's archivist rather than its sacrifice.
about_author: Ada Zhou is the pen name of a former field linguist who spent three winters recording disappearing folk traditions across northern mountain villages. She writes horror about archives, inheritance, and the things communities agree never to say twice.

chapters.title: The Songs They Sing Once
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. He arrives in Hollowmere during first snow, welcomed too warmly for a stranger, and records a carol the singers refuse to repeat, going pale when he asks them to. Settling into his inherited house, he notices the mirrors lag by a heartbeat. Emotional beat: uneasy wonder curdling into the sense of being watched by something patient.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The mirror-lag worsens, showing him moments before they occur — a door opening, a figure at the stair. Digging into the house's papers, he finds his great-grandfather's ledger: lists of winter guests who 'stayed on,' their names struck through. Emotional beat: scholarly curiosity turning to dread as documentation becomes evidence against his own bloodline.

chapters.title: What the Village Owes
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, with an interlude from innkeeper Maren Hale. Confronted, Maren confesses the founders' bargain: one outsider each winter, freely sung into the house, or the village starves and freezes as it once did. The villagers he befriended helped choose him. Emotional beat: betrayal and grief colliding with a horrifying temptation — the house shows him a life of warm belonging if he consents.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. On solstice night the villagers gather to sing him in, but Coral seizes the song, singing the founders' final verse backward with everything he has documented — the house's true name, its loneliness, its long service. The ritual inverts; the mirrors catch up and then go dark. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into fierce compassion, ending with Coral choosing to stay, alive, as keeper of the house's memory.
